description: Test your knowledge of PA HB1 | Hepatobiliary System.

cards.text: What are the two main sources of bilirubin, and what percentage does each contribute?
cards.answer: 80% from senescent RBC breakdown in the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, Kupffer cells, bone marrow); 20% from premature erythroblast destruction and turnover of non-haemoglobin haem proteins (myoglobin, cytochrome P450).

tip.tip: Remember 80-20 rule: RBCs are the major source, but 'other haems' contribute 20%

cards.text: Name the two enzymes that convert haem to unconjugated bilirubin and their products.
cards.answer: Haem oxygenase (RES macrophages) opens the porphyrin ring → biliverdin + CO. Biliverdin reductase reduces biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin (indirect bilirubin).

tip.tip: Haem → Biliverdin → Bilirubin: two reduction enzymes, two steps

cards.text: Why must unconjugated bilirubin bind to albumin in plasma? What is the danger of free UCB?
cards.answer: UCB is hydrophobic and water-insoluble; albumin binding allows plasma transport. Free UCB is neurotoxic, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and causes kernicterus.

tip.tip: UCB = lipophilic (fat-soluble) → needs protein carrier → free UCB damages brain

cards.text: What transporters on the hepatocyte basolateral membrane remove bilirubin from albumin?
cards.answer: OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (organic anion transporting polypeptides) actively transport UCB into the hepatocyte.

tip.tip: OATP = Organic Anion Transporter Polypeptide; remember it's on the 'sinusoidal' side of the hepatocyte

cards.text: Which enzyme conjugates unconjugated bilirubin, and what is added to form conjugated bilirubin?
cards.answer: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) in the smooth ER adds two molecules of glucuronic acid to UCB, producing bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated/direct bilirubin).

tip.tip: UGT1A1 = the conjugation enzyme; 'diglucuronide' = two glucuronic acids added

cards.text: What is the rate-limiting step in bilirubin clearance, and which protein defect causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome?
cards.answer: Active transport of conjugated bilirubin across the canalicular membrane via MRP2 (multidrug resistance protein 2/ABCC2) is the rate-limiting step. MRP2 mutations cause Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

tip.tip: MRP2 defect = Dubin-Johnson; remember: canalicular export is the bottleneck

cards.text: How is conjugated bilirubin converted in the colon, and what is the normal urinary urobilinogen level?
cards.answer: Colonic bacteria deconjugate CB → urobilinogen (colourless) → stercobilin (brown, stool pigment). ~20% of urobilinogen is reabsorbed; ~1% escapes into urine (normal: trace amounts detectable).

tip.tip: Bacteria do the work: CB → Urobilinogen → Stercobilin; most is reabsorbed (enterohepatic loop)

cards.text: At what serum bilirubin level does jaundice become clinically detectable, and when is scleral icterus visible?
cards.answer: Jaundice becomes visible at total bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL. Scleral icterus appears at 1.5–2 mg/dL because the sclera has high elastin affinity for bilirubin.

tip.tip: Sclera yellows first (elastin sticky for bilirubin) at 1.5–2; skin jaundice at 2.5+
